drivers.driver: Equity earnings yields remain structurally unattractive compared to nominal risk-free Treasury yields.
The lack of scalable, wonderful businesses at prices offering a sufficient margin of safety limits deployment.
Large cash and bill holdings preserve liquidity for future opportunistic investment without forecasting a market decline.

final.memo:
Charlie and I have always maintained that we do not forecast the market; we simply evaluate whether prices in general offer a margin of safety that justifies our capital [D01]. Today, with the 10-year Treasury yielding 4.37% and the S&P 500 earnings yield at roughly 3.51%, equities are not particularly cheap relative to risk-free nominal claims [D04]. While a 2.32% drawdown from recent highs is a trivial event, it does not suggest the sort of widespread pessimism or crisis pricing that would tempt us to move aggressively [D04, D06].

We continue to hold a significant cash position, which serves as a necessary buffer for our insurance operations and a reservoir for whenever Mr. Market eventually offers us a wonderful business at a fair price [D01, D08]. We feel no institutional imperative to force a purchase simply because our cash balance has grown; indeed, we would rather wait years for a high-conviction idea than risk permanent loss of capital on mediocre assets at excessive valuations [D04, D05]. Our focus remains on the durability of the businesses we own and the patience required to deploy our capital only when the math is clearly in our favor [D01, D06].
